concepts.name: Solutions and their defining traits
concepts.why: A solution is a homogeneous mixture in which the solute particles are individually dispersed among the solvent’s, so its composition is uniform, its state is usually the solvent’s, and its solute never settles out. Almost any gas, liquid or solid can act as a solvent, so air and brass are solutions just as saltwater is.
concepts.evidence: Figure 11.2 shows potassium dichromate dispersing into a uniform orange solution, Table 11.1 lists solutions of every phase, and the text sets out the five defining traits.

concepts.name: Ideal solutions and matter dispersal
concepts.why: When the attractions between unlike particles are no different from those between like particles, a solution forms with no change in energy, and it forms anyway, driven by the increased dispersal of matter alone.
concepts.evidence: Figure 11.3 lets helium and argon mix through an opened stopcock, and the text extends the same picture to methanol with ethanol and pentane with hexane.

concepts.name: Dissolution as three steps
concepts.why: The formation of a solution may be viewed as separating the solute particles and the solvent particles, both endothermic, and then letting solute and solvent attract one another (solvation), which is exothermic. The balance of the three steps decides whether dissolving releases or absorbs heat.
concepts.evidence: Figure 11.4 draws the stepwise path beside the direct formation of the solution, and the text applies it to an ionic compound dissolving in water.

concepts.name: Heat released or absorbed on dissolving
concepts.why: A solute whose solvation releases more energy than its separation costs dissolves exothermically, as sodium hydroxide does; one whose separation costs more dissolves endothermically, as ammonium nitrate does, and it can still dissolve because of the increase in dispersal.
concepts.evidence: Figure 11.5’s instant cold pack, and the contrast between calcium carbonate, lye and ammonium nitrate in the text; exercises on KNO<sub>3</sub> growing cold as it dissolves.

concepts.name: Predict whether two substances form a solution
concepts.why: Naming the strongest attractions within the solute, within the solvent and between the two lets us predict whether they will mix and which solvent suits a solute.
concepts.evidence: End-of-section exercises ask for the most important attractions in several solutions and whether oil, isopropyl alcohol and potassium bromide dissolve better in water or heptane.

concepts.name: Electrolytes and nonelectrolytes
concepts.why: An electrolyte yields ions when it dissolves, so its solution conducts electricity; a nonelectrolyte yields none. A strong electrolyte yields ions essentially completely, a weak electrolyte only in small part.
concepts.evidence: Figure 11.6 lights a bulb brightly through KCl solution, dimly through acetic acid and not at all through ethanol.

concepts.name: Ion-dipole attraction
concepts.why: The electrostatic attraction between an ion and a polar molecule turns the negative oxygen ends of water molecules toward a cation and the positive hydrogen ends toward an anion, and it is what lets water pull ions out of a solid.
concepts.evidence: Figure 11.7 draws water molecules oriented around K<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> ions leaving the surface of solid KCl.

concepts.name: Ionic compounds dissociate
concepts.why: When an ionic compound dissolves, water surrounds and solvates its ions and they disperse through the solution, a physical change called dissociation. Ionic compounds dissociate nearly completely, so even a sparingly soluble one is a strong electrolyte.
concepts.evidence: The text follows solid KCl in water at the microscopic level, and an exercise asks which beaker best shows the ions of Fe(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>(aq).

concepts.name: Covalent electrolytes react with water
concepts.why: Some covalent compounds conduct once dissolved because their molecules react chemically with water to form ions: a strong acid such as HCl ionizes completely and is a strong electrolyte, while weak acids and bases ionize partly and are weak electrolytes.
concepts.evidence: The ionization of water itself, and HCl transferring H<sup>+</sup> to water to form hydronium and chloride ions, drawn in Lewis structures in the text.

concepts.name: Classify a solute as a strong, weak or nonelectrolyte
concepts.why: Whether a solute is ionic, a strong acid, a weak acid or base, or an unreactive covalent compound tells us how well its solution will conduct.
concepts.evidence: An exercise asks for the expected conductivity of NaOH, HCl, glucose and NH<sub>3</sub> solutions; others contrast water and benzene or hexane as solvents for ions.

concepts.name: Solubility, saturated and unsaturated solutions
concepts.why: The solubility of a solute is the maximum concentration it can reach in a solvent under given conditions when dissolution is at equilibrium. A solution at that concentration is saturated, one below it is unsaturated.
concepts.evidence: The text adds sugar to water until some remains undissolved however long it is stirred.

concepts.name: Supersaturated solutions
concepts.why: A solution can hold more solute than its solubility, a nonequilibrium state that ends in precipitation or loss of gas when it is disturbed. Cooling a saturated solution of a solid, or warming or depressurizing a solution of a gas, can prepare one.
concepts.evidence: An opened carbonated beverage going flat (Figure 11.10), the Lake Nyos disaster (Figure 11.12) and the sodium acetate hand warmer (Figure 11.17).

concepts.name: Gases grow less soluble as temperature rises
concepts.why: Since a gaseous solute has no solute-solute attraction to overcome, only its attraction to the solvent sets its solubility, and that solubility typically decreases as the temperature increases, which is why thermal pollution starves natural waters of oxygen.
concepts.evidence: Figure 11.8 plots the solubilities of methane, oxygen, carbon monoxide, nitrogen and helium falling from 0 °C to 30 °C, and Figure 11.9 shows bubbles in warming water and a fish kill.

concepts.name: Henry’s law
concepts.why: The quantity of an ideal gas that dissolves in a definite volume of liquid is directly proportional to the pressure of the gas, $C_{\text{g}} = kP_{\text{g}}$, with k set by the gas, the solvent and the temperature. A gas that reacts with the solvent, as ammonia does with water, dissolves more than the law predicts.
concepts.evidence: The carbonated beverage of Figure 11.10 and the diver’s blood in the note on decompression sickness.

concepts.name: Calculate a gas solubility with Henry’s law
concepts.why: Finding k from one known solubility and pressure gives the solubility at any other pressure, and a constant read from a solubility graph answers whether a stream holds enough oxygen for its fish.
concepts.evidence: Examples 11.1 and 11.2 with their Check Your Learning, and the keyed exercises on O<sub>2</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub>.

concepts.name: Miscible, immiscible and partially miscible liquids
concepts.why: Liquids of similar polarity mix in all proportions because the attractions between unlike molecules are as strong as those between like ones, an illustration of “like dissolves like”; a nonpolar liquid and water form separate layers, and some pairs are only partially miscible.
concepts.evidence: Antifreeze and water (Figure 11.13), oil floating on water (Figure 11.14), and bromine and water forming two saturated layers (Figure 11.15).

concepts.name: Solubility curves of solids
concepts.why: The solubilities of most solids in water increase with temperature, though some, such as cerium sulfate, decrease, and a solubility curve reads off how much of a solid dissolves in 100 g of water at any temperature.
concepts.evidence: Figure 11.16 plots the solubility curves of sugar and seven salts from 0 °C to 100 °C, and an exercise reads KBr’s solubility at 10 °C from it.

concepts.name: Colligative properties
concepts.why: Vapor pressure lowering, boiling point elevation, freezing point depression and osmotic pressure depend only on the total concentration of solute particles, not on their identity, mass or size.
concepts.evidence: The text compares 1 m solutions of sucrose and ethylene glycol, which boil at the same temperature because each holds one mole of solute particles per kilogram of water.

concepts.name: Molality and mole fraction
concepts.why: Mole fraction is a component’s moles divided by the total moles, and molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent; both are built from masses and moles, so, unlike molarity, they do not change with temperature, and each can be converted into the others.
concepts.evidence: Examples 11.3 to 11.5 compute the mole fraction and molality of antifreeze, convert molality to mole fraction, and convert molarity to molality through a density.

concepts.name: Raoult’s law and vapor pressure lowering
concepts.why: The partial pressure of a component of an ideal solution is its mole fraction times the vapor pressure of the pure component, so a nonvolatile solute lowers the vapor pressure of the solvent in proportion to how much it dilutes the solvent.
concepts.evidence: Figure 11.18 contrasts evaporation from pure water and from a solution, and Example 11.6 computes the vapor pressure of glycerin in ethanol.

concepts.name: Distillation
concepts.why: The vapor above a mixture of two volatile liquids is richer in the more volatile one, so heating the mixture and condensing the vapor separates them; a fractionating column repeats the separation many times over.
concepts.evidence: The laboratory still of Figure 11.19 and the crude-oil column of Figure 11.20; Exercise 65 computes the enriched vapor of a methanol-ethanol solution.

concepts.name: Boiling point elevation
concepts.why: Because a nonvolatile solute lowers the vapor pressure, the solution must be hotter than the pure solvent before its vapor pressure reaches the atmosphere’s, and the elevation is proportional to the molality of all solute species, $\Delta T_{\text{b}} = K_{\text{b}}m$.
concepts.evidence: Table 11.2 lists K<sub>b</sub> for five solvents, Examples 11.7 and 11.8 compute boiling points, and Figure 11.23 shows the solution’s liquid-vapor curve lying beneath the solvent’s.

concepts.name: Freezing point depression
concepts.why: A solution freezes at a lower temperature than its pure solvent, by an amount proportional to the molality of all solute species, $\Delta T_{\text{f}} = K_{\text{f}}m$, because only the solvent freezes out; salted roads and antifreeze exploit it.
concepts.evidence: Example 11.9, the note on de-icing (Figures 11.21 and 11.22), and Figure 11.23’s solid-liquid curve displaced to the left.

concepts.name: Osmosis and osmotic pressure
concepts.why: Solvent diffuses through a semipermeable membrane into a solution faster than it returns, until the solution’s rising pressure equalizes the rates; that pressure is the osmotic pressure, $\Pi = MRT$. Applying more pressure reverses osmosis, and a cell swells or shrivels in a hypotonic or hypertonic solution.
concepts.evidence: The U-tubes of Figures 11.24 and 11.25, reverse osmosis in Figure 11.26, red blood cells in Figure 11.27, and Example 11.10’s glucose infusion.

concepts.name: Determine a molar mass from a colligative property
concepts.why: A measured freezing point depression, boiling point elevation or osmotic pressure gives the moles of solute in a known mass, and so the solute’s molar mass.
concepts.evidence: Example 11.11 from a freezing point in benzene and Example 11.12 from the osmotic pressure of hemoglobin, with their Check Your Learning.

concepts.name: Colligative properties of electrolytes and the van’t Hoff factor
concepts.why: An electrolyte yields more than one particle per formula unit, so its colligative effects are multiplied by the van’t Hoff factor i, the moles of particles per mole of formula units; residual attraction between ions, even ion pairs, makes the measured i smaller than predicted.
concepts.evidence: Table 11.3 sets predicted beside measured factors for 0.050 m solutions, Figure 11.28 draws ion pairs, and Example 11.13 finds the freezing point of a seawater-like NaCl solution.

concepts.name: Colloids between solutions and suspensions
concepts.why: A colloid’s particles are larger than most molecules yet small enough not to settle, so a colloid is intermediate between a solution, whose particles are molecules or ions, and a suspension, whose particles settle; colloidal particles scatter light, the Tyndall effect.
concepts.evidence: Figure 11.29 sets saltwater, milk and mud side by side, and Figure 11.30 shows searchlight beams made visible by fog and smoke.

concepts.name: Dispersed phase and dispersion medium
concepts.why: A colloid’s minor, particulate component is the dispersed phase and the substance it is spread through is the dispersion medium, and nearly every combination of states occurs: sols, aerosols, emulsions, foams and gels.
concepts.evidence: Table 11.4 names the colloidal systems by their phases, the gelatin dessert of Figure 11.37 is a gel, and an exercise asks for the phases of starch, smoke, fog, pearl and more.

concepts.name: Preparing colloids and emulsions
concepts.why: Colloidal particles are made by dispersion, grinding larger particles down, or by condensation, growing them from molecules or ions; an emulsion of two immiscible liquids is kept from separating by an emulsifying agent.
concepts.evidence: Paint pigments, clouds, the iron(III) hydroxide and gold sols, and milk and mayonnaise with their emulsifying agents, in the text.

concepts.name: How soaps and detergents clean
concepts.why: Soap and detergent molecules are amphiphilic, a nonpolar hydrocarbon end and an ionic end, so they gather at the boundary between grease and water and suspend the grease as colloidal particles that wash away.
concepts.evidence: Figures 11.31 and 11.32 draw soap and detergent molecules, Figure 11.33 an emulsified drop of oil, and the Deepwater Horizon note the dispersant sprayed on the spill.

concepts.name: Colloidal particles are charged
concepts.why: The particles of one colloid carry charges of the same sign, which keeps them dispersed by repulsion, and highly charged electrodes attract, neutralize and deposit them, as in the Cottrell precipitator that cleans smoke.
concepts.evidence: Iron(III) hydroxide particles bearing a positive charge, and Frederick Cottrell’s precipitator in Figures 11.35 and 11.36.
